title: When a request reaches the gateway and the target service is down, how do you handle it (circuit breaker, fallback, cache, retry/backoff, service discovery, feature flags)?
shortTitle: Handling a request when the target service is down

s1_definition.profdef: When a target service is unavailable, the gateway must fail gracefully rather than hang or crash. The standard toolkit is layered: service discovery and client-side load balancing first try another healthy instance; a retry with exponential backoff and jitter handles transient blips; a circuit breaker stops hammering a service that is genuinely down and fails fast; a fallback returns a safe default or a cached response so the client still gets something useful; and feature flags let operators disable or degrade a feature at runtime. The goal is bounded, predictable failure that protects the overall system.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh goes to the loans counter at National Bank of India but the loan officer has stepped out. A well-run bank does not make him stand there forever. First the receptionist checks if another loan officer at a nearby counter is free, that is trying another instance. If the first officer is only briefly away, the receptionist waits a short, growing moment and checks again, that is retry with backoff. If the whole loans department is shut for the day, the receptionist stops sending people there and immediately says so, that is the circuit breaker. And she can hand Rajesh yesterday's printed interest-rate sheet so he is not empty-handed, that is a cached fallback.
s1_definition.oneliner: When a service is down, try another instance, retry transient blips with backoff, open a circuit breaker to fail fast, and return a cached or default fallback so the client always gets a bounded, graceful response.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** When a target service is unavailable, the gateway must fail gracefully rather than hang or crash. The standard toolkit is layered: service discovery and client-side load balancing first try another healthy instance; a retry with exponential backoff and jitter handles transient blips; a circuit breaker stops hammering a service that is genuinely down and fails fast; a fallback returns a safe default or a cached response so the client still gets something useful; and feature flags let operators disable or degrade a feature at runtime. The goal is bounded, predictable failure that protects the overall system.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh goes to the loans counter at National Bank of India but the loan officer has stepped out. A well-run bank does not make him stand there forever. First the receptionist checks if another loan officer at a nearby counter is free, that is trying another instance. If the first officer is only briefly away, the receptionist waits a short, growing moment and checks again, that is retry with backoff. If the whole loans department is shut for the day, the receptionist stops sending people there and immediately says so, that is the circuit breaker. And she can hand Rajesh yesterday's printed interest-rate sheet so he is not empty-handed, that is a cached fallback.

**One line to remember:** When a service is down, try another instance, retry transient blips with backoff, open a circuit breaker to fail fast, and return a cached or default fallback so the client always gets a bounded, graceful response.

sections.s2_technical:
The first line of defense is service discovery with client-side load balancing. A service usually runs as several instances registered in a registry like Eureka. When the gateway needs the account service, it asks the registry for the live instances and the load balancer picks one. If that instance is down, the next call naturally lands on another healthy instance, so a single dead instance causes almost no visible failure.

The second line is retry with exponential backoff and jitter, for transient failures. A brief network blip or a momentary garbage-collection pause can fail one call that would succeed on the next. The gateway retries a small, bounded number of times, waiting longer between each attempt, for example 100 milliseconds, then 200, then 400, with a little randomness so many clients do not retry in lockstep. The key is that retries must be bounded and should only apply to idempotent operations, because retrying a money transfer blindly could double-charge Rajesh.

The third line is the circuit breaker, for sustained failures. If a service keeps failing, retrying just wastes resources and adds load to an already struggling service. A circuit breaker watches the failure rate; once failures cross a threshold it "opens" and immediately fails fast without even attempting the call, which protects both the caller and the struggling service. After a cool-down it goes "half-open" and lets a few trial calls through; if they succeed it "closes" and resumes normal traffic. In Resilience4j this is `@CircuitBreaker(name = "accountService", fallbackMethod = "fallback")`.

The fourth line is the fallback, which decides what the client actually receives when all else fails. The fallback can return a cached value, such as the last known balance; a sensible default, such as an empty list; or a clear, friendly error with the right status code. The fallback is what turns a scary failure into a graceful degradation. For example `public Balance fallback(String id, Throwable t) { return cache.get(id); }`.

The fifth tool is caching, which doubles as both a performance feature and a resilience feature. If the gateway caches recent responses, it can serve stale-but-useful data when the backend is down, which is often acceptable for read-heavy, slowly changing data like interest rates or a dashboard summary.

The sixth tool is feature flags, which let operators change behavior at runtime without a deploy. If a downstream service is being drained for maintenance, an operator flips a flag so the gateway routes around it or returns a maintenance message, rather than relying on failures to trigger fallbacks.

A senior nuance is that these layers combine and must be ordered correctly: discovery and load balancing first, then a short bounded retry, then the circuit breaker wrapping the whole thing, then the fallback. Also critical is timeout discipline; every downstream call needs an aggressive timeout, because the worst failure is not an error but a hang, where threads pile up waiting on a dead service and the gateway itself collapses.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's mobile dashboard asks the gateway for Rajesh's current balance, which lives in the Balance Service. One evening the Balance Service has a bad deployment and starts failing every request. Without protection, the gateway keeps calling it, each call hangs until timeout, threads pile up, and soon the entire gateway becomes unresponsive, so even healthy features like viewing card details break. This is the classic cascading failure a circuit breaker prevents.

Problem 2 — Sometimes the failure is not total; it is a brief blip because one instance restarted. In that case, retrying once or twice with a short wait would succeed, and opening the circuit would be an overreaction. We need to distinguish transient blips, handled by retry, from sustained outages, handled by the circuit breaker.

The connection to the fix: we will build a `BalanceGateway` that calls a flaky `BalanceService`. It wraps the call in a bounded retry for transient failures, a circuit breaker that opens after a failure threshold, and a fallback that returns the last cached balance. The demo drives the service through healthy, blip, and fully-down phases so the reader sees each mechanism activate.

What the code will do. There is a `BalanceService` whose health we can toggle to simulate blips and outages. There is a `CircuitBreaker` with closed, open, and half-open states. There is a `BalanceCache` holding the last known balance. There is a `BalanceGateway` that orchestrates retry, circuit breaker, and fallback. The demo requests Rajesh's balance repeatedly while the service transitions from healthy to a blip to a full outage, and logs which mechanism served each response.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is repeated requests for Rajesh's balance at SAV2001 while the Balance Service moves through healthy, blip, down, and recovered phases.

Step 1. In the healthy phase, the circuit is closed so the request is allowed. The first attempt succeeds, the breaker records success, and the balance of one million rupees is cached and returned. The cache is now warm.

Step 2. In the blip phase, the first attempt throws a transient error. The gateway waits 100 milliseconds and retries; the second attempt succeeds, so the retry quietly absorbed the blip. The client never sees a failure, and the circuit stays closed.

Step 3. In the outage phase, every attempt fails. On the first request, all three retries fail, the breaker records a failure, and the gateway returns the cached balance as a fallback. After enough failed requests reach the threshold, the breaker opens.

Step 4. Once the breaker is open, new requests are not even attempted. The gateway fails fast and immediately returns the cached balance without touching the dead service. This is what prevents threads from piling up and protects the gateway from collapsing.

Step 5. After the cool-down, the breaker goes half-open and lets one trial request through. In the recovered phase that trial succeeds, so the breaker closes and normal traffic resumes, now serving fresh balances again. Throughout the whole journey, the client always received a usable balance, either fresh or recently cached.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Request: getBalance("SAV2001")
    │
    ▼
  ┌─ Circuit Breaker ─┐
  │ state?            │
  └───────┬───────────┘
          │
   OPEN?  ├──────────────────────────→ fail fast → cache fallback (Rs. last known)
          │
   CLOSED/HALF-OPEN
          ▼
  ┌─ Retry (max 3, backoff 100/200/400ms) ─┐
  │  attempt → BalanceService.getBalance    │
  │     success? ── yes ─→ cache.put + return fresh
  │     fail → wait, retry                  │
  │     all fail → recordFailure            │
  └───────┬─────────────────────────────────┘
          ▼
   all retries failed
          │
          ▼
   cache.get("SAV2001")  → Rs. last known balance (fallback)
          │
   (after threshold failures → breaker OPENS)
          │
   (after cool-down → HALF_OPEN → trial → success → CLOSED)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
When a request reaches the gateway and the target service is down, the goal is to fail gracefully and in a bounded way, never to hang or cascade. I handle it with a layered toolkit, and the order of the layers matters. The first layer is service discovery with client-side load balancing, because most services run as several instances, so if one instance is dead the load balancer simply picks a healthy one and the failure is invisible. The second layer is a bounded retry with exponential backoff and a little jitter, which quietly absorbs transient blips like a brief network hiccup or a one-instance restart. I only retry idempotent reads, because blindly retrying a money transfer could double-charge the customer.

The third layer is the circuit breaker, which handles sustained outages. In my banking work at National Bank of India, the Balance Service once had a bad deployment and started failing every request. Without protection, the gateway kept calling it, each call hung until timeout, threads piled up, and the whole gateway became unresponsive, which also broke healthy features like viewing card details. The circuit breaker fixes exactly this: it watches the failure rate, and once failures cross a threshold it opens and fails fast without even attempting the call, which protects both the gateway and the already-struggling service. After a cool-down it goes half-open and lets one trial call through, and if that succeeds it closes and normal traffic resumes.

The fourth layer is the fallback, which decides what the client actually receives. I serve the last known balance from the cache, so instead of an error the customer sees a slightly stale but perfectly usable number, which for a read-heavy dashboard is a good trade. The fallback can also be a sensible default or a clear, friendly error with the correct status code. This is what turns a scary outage into a graceful degradation.

On top of those, I keep two operational tools. Caching doubles as resilience, because it lets me serve stale-but-useful data for slowly changing information. And feature flags let an operator route around a service or show a maintenance message at runtime, without waiting for failures to trigger fallbacks and without a redeploy. The nuance I always add is timeout discipline, because the worst failure mode is not an error, it is a hang. Every downstream call gets an aggressive timeout, so a dead service produces a fast, clean failure that the circuit breaker and fallback can handle, rather than a slow strangulation of the gateway's threads.
